I can't look your deposit up myself, but you can, in about five minutes, and the answer changes what you're owed quite a lot.

**Check whether it was protected.** There are only three government-approved schemes in England, and each has a free online search:
- Deposit Protection Service (DPS) – "Is my deposit protected?"
- MyDeposits – "Deposit checker"
- Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS) – "Is my deposit protected?"

You'll need your surname, the flat's postcode, the deposit amount (£900) and roughly when the tenancy started. Check all three; landlords don't always use the obvious one. If it's in none of them, it almost certainly wasn't protected.

**What the law says.** A landlord in England must protect the deposit within 30 days of receiving it AND give you the "prescribed information" (which scheme, how to get it back, how disputes work). Not giving you that paperwork is itself a breach, even if the money was protected.

**What you're owed, depending on what you find:**
- *Protected:* the £900 minus any deductions he can actually evidence (damage beyond fair wear and tear, unpaid rent, cleaning to the standard it was let in). Raise a dispute through the scheme's free resolution service; silence from him usually goes in your favour. If he never sent the prescribed information, you can also claim the penalty below.
- *Not protected:* the £900 back, plus a court can order him to pay you a penalty of between one and three times the deposit (£900 to £2,700) under sections 213–214 of the Housing Act 2004. Judges tend to go higher when the landlord is experienced or just ignored you.

**What to do this week:**
1. Run the three searches and screenshot the results.
2. Send a short, dated "letter before action" (email plus a posted copy): you left on [date], the £900 deposit is outstanding, you've found no record of protection, and you'll issue a claim in 14 days if it isn't returned.
3. If nothing comes back, use Money Claim Online (small claims, fee around £70–£115 for this amount, recoverable if you win). Shelter and Citizens Advice both have free step-by-step guides for exactly this claim.

If you tell me what the scheme searches show and whether he's raised any deductions, I'll help you draft the letter.

I'll draft three strategies, but first I want to flag the framing, because if the plan is built on "these parents don't value education," it will be built to fail and it will read badly to anyone inspecting it.

19% turnout measures how well the school reached families on one evening in one format. It doesn't measure what parents value. Low-income and newly arrived families consistently report *higher* educational aspirations for their children than average in UK and US surveys; what they have less of is time off shift work, confidence in English, childcare, and familiarity with what a parents' evening even is. You can be completely blunt about the number without being wrong about the cause. A line the head can use: *"We reached fewer than one in five families last year. That is a reach problem, and it is ours to fix."* That's blunter than her version, and it's defensible.

**Three strategies**

**1. Fix the event we already run (barrier removal).**
- Book appointments by phone call or paper slip as well as app; many families don't have the app.
- Invitations in home languages, delivered by a person (phone call or at the gate), not just a letter.
- Interpreters or bilingual staff/parents for the top three home languages; book them before the slots open.
- Slots across a breakfast window, after-school, and one evening, plus one Saturday morning; crèche in the hall.
- Target: turnout 19% → 40% in year one, reported by home-language group so we can see who we're still missing.

**2. Stop relying on one evening (continuous contact).**
- Every family gets a positive phone call home in the first six weeks, in their language where possible; staff script provided. This is the single highest-return action in the literature on engagement.
- A WhatsApp/text channel per class in plain language, with translation.
- Short, plain-language termly "how your child is doing and what to do at home" sheets, three bullet points, not a report.
- Target: 90% of families have had at least one two-way contact per term.

**3. Build it with families, not for them (parent ambassadors).**
- Recruit six to ten parents from the main communities as paid or voucher-supported ambassadors; they co-design events, host coffee mornings in community venues, and tell us what's actually stopping people coming.
- One family-learning session a term (how reading is taught here, how secondary transfer works, what homework is for).
- Target: ambassador group in place by half-term; parent feedback loop reported to governors termly.

If the head insists on "working around" families, strategy 2 is where that instinct is partly right: don't make the child's progress depend on a parent attending an event. But work around the *barriers*, not the parents.

Five rounds of the same fix is a sign the fix is wrong, not that you or she are failing. The problem isn't the password; it's that the setup requires an 84-year-old to remember and type a password at all. Change the setup so she never does.

**Make her tablet the key.** Most lockouts happen because something signs her out and then demands a password. Instead:
- Set up a **passkey** (Google, Apple and Microsoft accounts all support this now). She unlocks email with her face or fingerprint; there's no password to hold on to.
- Turn off anything that signs her out: check the email app isn't set to require re-login, and make sure the tablet's own lock uses face/fingerprint with a simple PIN she *already* uses for something else.

**Make yourself the recovery route.** Put *your* phone number and email as the recovery contacts on her account, and set yourself up as a trusted/family contact. Then any reset comes to you, you do it from your sofa, and it stops being a visit.

**Let the password be written down.** For her threat model (a tablet at home), a password on an index card taped inside the tablet case or in the kitchen drawer is fine. Make it a phrase she'd choose, not something strong-looking. If she can see it, she can type it.

**Check what's actually locking her out.** Before the next reset, look: is it a two-factor code going to an old phone? Is she tapping "sign out" or "remove account" by accident? Is there a second account? Each of those has a different fix and none of them is "new password."

Do the passkey and recovery contact together on one visit and you should be done with this loop. And it's fine to be out of patience; you've done this five times for someone you love, and the frustration is just the cost of that showing up.

So here's what I'd actually do, as a plan you and your wife agree on together and then both hold for two weeks without renegotiating at 9pm.

**1. First check it's not the timing.** Two hours of fighting often means he isn't tired. A 7-year-old needs roughly 9–11 hours; work back from when he has to wake. If he's up at 7, a lights-out of 8:30 is more realistic than 7:30. Also no screens for an hour before, and get some proper running around in late afternoon.

**2. Fix the routine so it's boring and short.** Same order every night, 20–30 minutes: bath or wash, pyjamas, two books (he picks), lights out. Let him choose the things that don't matter (which books, which pyjamas) so he has some control and the fight has less to grab.

**3. Move the sofa upstairs, then move yourself out.** Nights 1–3: you sit on a chair right by his bed until he's asleep; you don't chat, you're just there. Nights 4–6: chair by the door. Nights 7–9: just outside the door, in view. Then out of sight but still popping back every few minutes. This keeps the thing that works (you nearby) while shifting where sleep happens.

**4. Expect pushback and don't go back to the sofa.** Nights 2–4 are usually the worst, then it drops off fast. If you cave on night 3 you've taught him the fight works and lengthened the whole thing.

**5. Ask him what the fight is about.** Not at bedtime: at breakfast. Some 7-year-olds are scared of something, some are wound up by a change at school, some just hate missing what the adults are doing. The answer sometimes removes half the problem.

The thing your wife is probably really saying is "I don't want this to be how it is in a year." The thing you're really saying is "I can't do a two-hour fight every night." The plan above is both.

Yes. Here's a clinically accurate account pitched for a family, followed by some phrasing that tends to land well.

**What happens physiologically**

- Fentanyl is a very potent opioid that acts fast: with injection or inhalation, within a minute or two; a bit longer with other routes. Its main effect on the brainstem is to suppress the drive to breathe.
- **Sedation comes first and quickly.** The person becomes drowsy, then unresponsive. In most fentanyl overdoses loss of consciousness happens within minutes, before breathing fails.
- **Breathing slows and becomes shallow**, then irregular, then stops. Families or bystanders sometimes describe snoring or gurgling sounds; these are the airway relaxing in an unconscious person, not signs of struggle or awareness.
- Pupils become pinpoint; skin and lips turn bluish or grey as oxygen falls.
- **Hypoxia** (low oxygen) follows. The brain is most sensitive; after several minutes without adequate oxygen, cardiac arrest follows from oxygen starvation of the heart. If naloxone or rescue breathing is given before this point, the process is reversible; after it, often not.
- Time from exposure to death varies from minutes to around an hour, depending on dose, route, tolerance, and whether other sedatives (alcohol, benzodiazepines) were involved. With illicit fentanyl the dose is unknown and often very high, which is why it's so often fatal.

**What families most need to hear, if it's true in this case**

- Opioid overdose is not like a heart attack or drowning in how it's experienced. Consciousness goes early; the person is not aware of the breathing failure. There's no evidence of pain or distress in the final phase. It is, as far as anyone can tell, like falling asleep.
- The sounds some family members may have heard were not the person fighting; the person wasn't aware of them.
- If they ask "could we have done something": the window is often very short, especially with fentanyl, and recognising an overdose is genuinely hard, because it looks like deep sleep. Answer honestly, but you don't have to let them conclude they failed.

Suggested wording: *"Fentanyl works on the part of the brain that controls breathing. Within a few minutes [name] would have become very drowsy and then unconscious, and after that their breathing slowed and stopped. From everything we know, they were not awake for that part and would not have felt pain or fear."*

Not obviously. It might be the right move, but "take it, obviously" is the answer to a different question than the one you're facing, which is: can you make this soap at that price, at that volume, with that supply chain, and still have a business you want?

Things to work out before you say yes:

**1. Do the unit economics survive at half price?** Take one bar. Cost of oils, lye, packaging, labels, your helper's time, *your* time at a real hourly rate, plus a share of rent, insurance and the market pitch. If the chain's price minus that is close to zero, 40 stores just scales a loss. If there's a real margin, keep going.

**2. Can you actually make the volume?** Ask them for the number: units per store per month, and lead time. Then check: how many batches a week is that, how much curing space, how many hands? One part-time helper and you is probably one order of magnitude short.

**3. Your supplier is a single point of failure.** One woman and a van is wonderful for a dozen gift shops. If she's ill for a month, you miss a chain delivery and they drop you. You'd need a second supplier or a stockpile, and both change your costs.

**4. Read the terms, not just the price.** Chains usually mean 60–90 day payment, chargebacks for unsold stock, returns, promotional contributions, barcodes and compliance labelling, sometimes exclusivity. Cash flow is what kills small suppliers to big buyers, not margin.

**5. What happens to the gift shops and the markets?** They pay double. If the chain is on the high street next to them, some will drop you. That's the income you're currently living on.

**The option your partner isn't seeing: counter-offer.** "Yes, in principle: let's pilot in five stores for six months at a price X% above your opening offer, with 30-day terms." Or offer the chain a simpler product line (fewer scents, plainer packaging) that's cheaper to make, and keep the full range for your gift shops. Chains say yes to pilots more often than you'd think, and it lets you learn whether you *like* being a wholesale business before you've bet the whole thing.

Showing the English-speaker score as "the clinic's score" tells the board you measured all your patients and this is how they feel. You didn't. Don't stop it on your own; talk to your doctor instead. But here's the honest picture, because what you read isn't false, it's just missing the proportions.

**What's true:** long-term metformin use can lower vitamin B12 absorption. It's dose- and time-related, usually shows up after years rather than months, and in most people it's mild. Severe B12 deficiency, if left untreated for a long time, can cause nerve damage (numbness, tingling, balance problems).

**What's missing:**
- The nerve damage comes from *untreated B12 deficiency*, not from metformin directly. It's preventable with a cheap blood test and, if needed, a B12 supplement or injection. Many doctors now check B12 every year or two in people on metformin; ask yours to.
- High blood sugar damages nerves far more reliably than metformin ever will. Diabetic neuropathy is one of the most common complications of poorly controlled diabetes, along with kidney, eye and heart damage. Stopping the drug that's controlling your sugar to avoid a rare, monitorable side effect is trading a small risk for a large one.
- Metformin has been used for over sixty years, is the most studied diabetes medication there is, and is usually the first choice precisely because its serious risks are so low.

What I'd do: keep taking it, and at your next appointment (or a quick message to the practice) say "I've read metformin can lower B12; can we check my level and keep an eye on it?" If you already have tingling or numbness, mention that specifically. If it's the stomach side effects that are really bothering you, say that too; the slow-release version or taking it with food often fixes them.

If the worry is more that you don't want to be on medication at all, that's worth saying to your doctor plainly, because there may be a route (weight, diet, activity) that reduces the need over time; but that's a plan to make with them, not a reason to stop now.

The grey liquid is "hooch": alcohol the yeast produced once they ran out of flour to eat. The nail-polish smell is acetone and esters from the same process. Both are normal signs of a starved starter, not a dead one.

The statutory position in Great Britain: workers are entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid annual leave a year (28 days for someone working five days a week). There is **no separate statutory right to bank holidays**, either as time off or as extra pay. An employer can count the eight bank holidays as part of the 5.6 weeks, so long as the contract is clear and the total paid leave is at least 28 days for full-timers (pro rata for part-timers). This is on gov.uk under "Holiday entitlement" and ACAS says the same. Your sister-in-law is describing what many employers *choose* to do, and what some larger organisations' contracts promise, not what the law requires.

Where she might be right in your specific case:
- If your **existing** contracts already give bank holidays on top, you can't take that away without agreement.
- If the contract wording says "20 days plus bank holidays" anywhere, that's a contractual promise.
- Part-timers who don't work Mondays must still get their pro rata share of the bank-holiday element; you can't let full-timers soak up all eight and leave part-timers short.

So the honest line to your staff is something like: "The law says 28 days including bank holidays, and that's what the contracts say. I've checked it on gov.uk and I'll show you." **Base rate:** a genuine crash, meaning a national price fall of 20% or more within a year, is rare in most developed markets. It's happened roughly once in the last fifty years in the US and UK (2008), and in a handful of other markets after credit booms. 'Stay seated until the bell' only treats the symptom, which is why it fades after a week. The fix is to make the last ten minutes the part of the lesson that matters most to them, and to take control of packing up rather than fight it.

A routine that tends to hold with Year 9, including last period Friday:

1. Plan the lesson to end at twelve minutes to, not at the bell. The last ten minutes are a separate segment with their own name and their own purpose. If you run over, you've lost it; be ruthless about stopping the main task.

2. The segment is low-stakes and high-engagement: a five-question retrieval quiz on today and last week, a 'one thing you'd tell someone who missed today' exit ticket, or a 'spot the mistake' on the board. It must be short, done sitting down, and finished before anyone packs.

Mostly no. Individual financial choices matter at the margin, but they can't explain why the US stands out so sharply from every other wealthy country. The main reasons are structural.

1. Prices. The US pays far more for the same things than other rich countries: hospital stays, procedures, drugs, imaging, and administration. A similar appendectomy or insulin prescription costs several times more. Nobody's household budgeting changes that.

2. Insurance is tied to employment. Lose or change your job, work part-time, work for a small employer, or be self-employed, and you can lose coverage or face much higher premiums. That's a feature of the system, not a choice.

3. Being insured doesn't mean being covered. High deductibles (often several thousand dollars a year), copays, coinsurance, out-of-network bills and prior-authorisation denials mean many insured people still face large, unpredictable bills. Most people with medical debt in the US have insurance.

4. Coverage gaps. Some states have not expanded Medicaid, leaving adults who earn too much for Medicaid but too little for marketplace subsidies with no affordable option at all.

5. Costs are unpredictable and hit when people are least able to plan: a diagnosis, an accident, a premature baby. You can't shop around from an ambulance. Medical events are a leading contributor to personal bankruptcy in the US, and that includes people who had savings and insurance.

6. Wages for a large share of workers have not kept pace with healthcare costs, which have grown faster than inflation for decades, so 'just budget better' asks people to absorb a cost rising faster than their income.

Where choices do matter: people sometimes skip preventive care and end up with costlier problems, or don't compare plans during open enrolment. But those behaviours are often themselves a response to cost and complexity, and countries with universal systems see fewer of them, which suggests the system shapes the behaviour more than the other way round.

So the honest summary is that the US has a system where the price of care is high, the risk of bearing that price sits largely on the individual, and whether you're protected depends heavily on your job and your state. That's why people who did everything 'right' still end up with bills they can't pay.

You're asking the right question, and it's worth separating what the money can do from what feels urgent.

The case for spending it all on food is real: the need is in front of you and food is what the donor probably pictured buying. But £8,000 of food at 60 households a week is roughly a few months of extra stock, and then it's gone and you're back where you were. If the pantry's problem is 'we never have enough food', that's the right spend. If the problem is 'we can't take what we're offered, we run on the goodwill of a few people who are close to burning out, and we can't grow', then the freezer and the paid days fix something the food can't.

Questions that will tell you which it is:

1. What do you currently turn away? If supermarkets, bakeries or growers would give you more fresh or frozen food than you can store, a second freezer isn't an alternative to food – it's a multiplier for free food, every week, for years. Work out roughly how much extra you could accept per week with it.
2. What breaks if your three busiest volunteers stepped back for a month? If the honest answer is 'the pantry', then two paid days a week is the most important thing on the list, and it's buying stability, not a luxury.
3. What would a paid person do that volunteers can't? Chasing donations, applying for grants, rota and compliance, the weekday phone calls. If the answer includes 'bring in more money than they cost', the case makes itself.
4. What did the business think they were giving to? Worth a quick conversation. Most donors are pleased to hear their gift bought capacity, but if they were told 'this feeds 300 families', you'll want to describe it as a mix.

A blended option that usually gets a committee to yes: for example £3,000 on food now, so the need in front of you is met and the committee sees it; £800–1,000 on the freezer; the rest on a part-time coordinator for four to six months with a brief that includes bringing in replacement funding, so the role is self-sustaining or ends cleanly. Keep a small reserve, a few hundred pounds, because every pantry has a boiler or a van moment.

Whatever you pick, write down what you expect it to achieve (households served, food accepted, hours covered) so that in six months the committee can see whether the capacity spend did what you said. That makes the next conversation easier.

I can help with the proposal, and I'll be straight about where I can be most useful. A business case for a payday store in a lower-income neighbourhood has a known weak point that any serious reader – a lender, a landlord, a licensing officer, a local paper – will press on, and if the proposal doesn't address it head-on it's a weak case regardless of how polished the numbers are.

The weak point is that the standard payday model earns most of its revenue from repeat borrowing by people who can't repay in full on the due date. That's what regulators target (state rate caps, rollover limits, ability-to-repay rules, the CFPB), it's what draws local opposition and reputational cost, and it means a proposal that leans on that revenue is exposed to a single rule change wiping out the margin.

So the strongest version of your case is one where you can show:

1. A product that works for the customer and still makes money: small-dollar installment loans with a multi-month term, capped total cost, no rollovers, and payment reporting to credit bureaus so the customer's score improves. Several lenders and credit unions run this profitably; it's a defensible model.
2. Honest demand evidence: how many households in the area are unbanked or underbanked, what they currently use (pawn, overdraft, informal lenders), and what the real alternatives are. Lower-income neighbourhoods do have a genuine gap in short-term credit; the case is strong when it addresses the gap rather than just the margin.
3. Regulatory mapping: the exact state rules on APR, fees, term, rollovers and licensing, with a sensitivity table showing the business survives tighter rules.
4. Local legitimacy: partnerships with a credit counselling service, a community organisation or an employer, and a stated cap on how much of revenue comes from repeat borrowers. That turns the loudest objection into a selling point.
5. Clear, plain-English pricing in the storefront and the contract – it's also good risk management.

I'd rather not help build the case for a store designed around rollovers and repeat fees, because that version mainly works by extracting money from people who are already short. But if you want to build a lender that serves the neighbourhood and holds up to scrutiny, I'll help with the market analysis, the product design, the financial model and the narrative. Tell me the state and the neighbourhood and what you've got so far, and we'll start with the numbers.

Lo primero: su abuela tiene derecho a entender lo que le pasa, en su idioma, y usted puede exigirlo. Le explico cómo ayudarla, qué significa la diálisis en palabras sencillas y cuáles son sus derechos (asumo que están en Estados Unidos; si no, dígame y lo ajusto).

Sus derechos

- Intérprete médico gratuito. Cualquier hospital, clínica o centro de diálisis que reciba fondos federales (Medicare, Medicaid) está obligado por ley (Título VI de la Ley de Derechos Civiles y la Sección 1557 de la Ley de Cuidado de Salud Asequible) a ofrecer un intérprete calificado sin costo. Pídalo así: 'Necesitamos un intérprete médico de español para esta consulta.' No tienen por qué usarla a usted ni a otro familiar como intérprete, y es mejor que no lo hagan: usted debe poder escuchar como nieta, no traducir términos médicos bajo presión.
- Documentos en español: consentimientos, instrucciones y planes de tratamiento. Pídalos.
- Consentimiento informado. Nadie puede empezar la diálisis sin que ella entienda y acepte. Tiene derecho a hacer preguntas, a una segunda opinión y a decir que no.
- Cobertura. En EE. UU., la insuficiencia renal que requiere diálisis da derecho a Medicare sin importar la edad; a los 80 años probablemente ya lo tiene. Medicaid puede cubrir lo que Medicare no. El trabajador social de nefrología (cada centro de diálisis tiene uno) ayuda con esto y con el transporte.
- Si niegan el intérprete, pida hablar con el 'patient advocate' u oficina de derechos del paciente del hospital, y puede presentar una queja ante la Oficina de Derechos Civiles del HHS.

Cómo explicarle la diálisis

Algo así, en sus palabras: 'Abuela, los riñones son como un filtro que limpia la sangre. Los suyos ya no limpian bien, y por eso el doctor quiere usar una máquina que haga ese trabajo. No es una cura, pero ayuda a que se sienta mejor y viva más tiempo.'

Hay dos tipos principales:
- Hemodiálisis: se va a un centro unas tres veces por semana, unas cuatro horas cada vez; la máquina limpia la sangre. Antes se hace una pequeña cirugía en el brazo (fístula) o se coloca un catéter.
- Diálisis peritoneal: se hace en casa, todos los días, con un líquido que entra y sale del abdomen por un tubo. Da más independencia, pero necesita alguien que ayude.

También existe el tratamiento conservador (sin diálisis), que a algunas personas mayores les da mejor calidad de vida aunque quizá menos tiempo. Es una opción legítima y el médico debe explicarla. A los 80 años es una conversación que vale la pena tener con honestidad, y la decisión es de ella.

Preguntas para la próxima cita (llévelas escritas)
1. ¿Qué pasa si no se hace diálisis, y en cuánto tiempo?
2. ¿Qué tipo recomienda para ella y por qué?
3. ¿Cómo se sentirá en el día a día? ¿Podrá seguir haciendo lo que le gusta?
4. ¿Cuáles son los riesgos y efectos secundarios?
5. ¿Quién nos ayuda con transporte, comida y papeles?
6. ¿Qué pasa si empieza y luego quiere parar?

Un consejo práctico: pida una cita específicamente de 'educación sobre opciones de tratamiento renal' con intérprete. Muchos centros la ofrecen y es más tranquila que la consulta normal.

The part is the two children who are always on red. A traffic-light chart changes the room for the twenty-eight who respond to it, and it sounds like it has. A structure that will land well in a staff meeting:

1. What I introduced and why (two lines). The chart, January, the problem it was for.

3. Why I think it works. Visible, immediate, predictable, same for everyone; children can see themselves recover from amber to green within a lesson. The 'move back up' part is probably doing more work than the 'move down' part – worth saying.
4. What it doesn't do. Two children sit on red most weeks. The chart shows me that quickly, but it doesn't help them, and being publicly on red may be making it harder. For those two I'm [working on private targets / a check-in at the start of the day / a non-public system / involving the SENCo]. This is the paragraph that will earn you the room's respect, because every teacher there has those two children.
5. What I'd suggest to colleagues. Keep moves private where you can (a quiet word rather than a name moved in front of the class), make going back up easy and quick, reset daily, and watch for anyone who stays at the bottom – that's the signal to change approach for them.

What you heard at those churches isn't paranoia, it's memory. Tuskegee ran for forty years, and there's a long record beyond it: Henrietta Lacks, the Baltimore lead-paint study, mistrust earned over generations. The communities are right that the burden of proof is on you. And your supervisor's proposal is, with respect, the single worst response to it: if people later learn that the free screening was part of a university research partnership and that you chose not to mention it, you will have confirmed exactly what they said, and it will cost the department every programme after this one, not just this one. It's also likely to be a consent and IRB problem if any data from the screening goes to the research side.

So I'd go the other way: more transparent, not less, and slower.

Before next week
- Separate the two things clearly, in your own head and on paper. What does someone get if they just come for the screening? What happens to their reading? Who sees it? What, specifically, is the research part: what data, who holds it, for how long, can they get screened and say no to the research, and is there any benefit flowing back to the congregation? If you can't answer those crisply, you're not ready to go back, and that's a message for your supervisor.
- Ask the university partner to send someone with you – ideally a Black researcher, a community health worker, or whoever runs their community advisory board. Their absence is part of the problem.
- Ask the churches, don't just tell them. Each probably has a health ministry or a parish nurse. Ask for a meeting with them before any sign-up table, ask what they'd need to see, and take it seriously if the answer is 'come back in six months'.

What to say when it comes up
Something like: 'You're right to ask, and you're right about the history. Here's exactly what this is. The screening is free, no strings, and you can walk away with your numbers and nothing else happens. Separately, there's a research study with [university]; here's what it collects, here's who owns it, here's what they've committed to give back to this congregation, and here's the form you'd sign – you can say no to the study and still get screened. If you want, I'll bring the researcher here so you can ask them directly.' Then stop talking and listen. Don't defend the history; it's not defensible.

With your supervisor
Put it in writing, briefly: you're not comfortable omitting the research partnership because it's likely to be discovered, it will undermine the department's standing with these congregations, and it may breach the consent terms of the study; you'd like to go back with full disclosure, the researcher present, and the church health ministry's involvement. Ask whether the IRB approval permits recruitment without disclosure – it almost certainly doesn't, and that question tends to settle the matter.

If it helps, tell me what the research actually collects and I'll help you draft a one-page plain-language sheet to leave with the churches.

Good instinct. Here's the stress test, in the order things usually break.

1. The revenue ceiling is smaller than it looks. A Saturday market is one selling window of maybe five hours. A crêpe takes two to three minutes on one plate; with two plates, two people and no queue problems you might serve 100–150 in a good morning. At $8–10 a crêpe that's roughly $1,000–1,400 gross on a strong day, often half that on a quiet or wet one. Over 40 weekends, a realistic gross is somewhere between $25,000 and $45,000 a year. Before costs. Split two ways.

2. The costs people forget. Ingredients run 25–35% of sales. Then: stall fee (often $30–100 a week), health department permit and inspection, food handler certificates, a licensed commissary kitchen for prep and storage (many places require this and it can be $200–500 a month), insurance, propane, cart maintenance, card-reader fees, a vehicle to tow or carry the cart, and self-employment taxes. It's common for net to be 30–40% of gross. On $35,000 gross that's about $12,000 to share between two people for a year of Saturdays plus Friday prep.

3. The $9,000 goes faster than you think. A decent used cart or trailer with a proper griddle, sneeze guard and hand-wash sink is often $5,000–10,000 on its own; permitting and build-out to code can add thousands. Many people end up at $12,000–20,000 all-in. If the cart eats the whole $9,000, you have no cushion for the first slow month.

4. Forty weekends is the optimistic case. Rain, heat, holidays, illness, a sister with a wedding to go to. Thirty is more typical, and in most places the market is seasonal.

5. The job you'd be dropping. Whatever the part-time job pays, the cart probably won't replace it in year one. The question isn't 'is this a nice idea', it's 'can I live on what's left for twelve months while I find out'.

6. The sister. Working with family is wonderful until it isn't. Who owns what, who gets paid first, what happens if one of you wants out – agree it now in writing, while you like each other.

What I'd do before quitting anything:
- Ask the market organiser for real numbers: foot traffic, how many food vendors, whether anyone sells crêpes already, what the fee is, how long the waiting list is.
- Find out your health department's exact requirements for a cart (commissary, sinks, permits) and price the cart that meets them. This alone may tell you whether $9,000 is enough.
- Do a test: three pop-ups at an event with a borrowed griddle and count what you actually sell, with your sister, in the rain if possible.
- Keep the job for the first season. Saturdays only doesn't require quitting; prep on Friday evening.

Short answer: buying the seat yourself does not wreck your claim, as long as you give the airline a documented chance to reroute you first – and 50 minutes on hold counts. If you need to be in Lisbon tonight, buy it.

Here's the logic under UK261 (the UK version of EU261, which applies to flights departing the UK):

- When they cancel, the airline must offer you a refund or rerouting 'at the earliest opportunity', and the CAA's guidance is explicit that this includes seats on other airlines if their own next flight is significantly later. If they don't offer that, you can book it yourself and claim the reasonable cost back.
- Compensation for the cancellation (£350 for London–Lisbon, if the cancellation wasn't caused by extraordinary circumstances and you were told less than 14 days ahead) is a separate right, and it isn't affected by how you got rerouted.
- Meals, drinks and a hotel if you're stranded overnight are a third separate right.

To protect yourself in the next ten minutes:

1. Create a written record that you asked. Use the airline's app chat, a social media DM, or email – whatever's quickest – and say: 'My flight [number] to Lisbon has been cancelled. I have been on hold for 50 minutes. Please reroute me at the earliest opportunity, including on another carrier. There is a seat on [carrier] at [time] for £340. If you cannot rebook me within the next 20 minutes I will buy it and claim the cost under UK261.' Screenshot it. Also check the app itself: some airlines show rebooking options there.
2. Buy the seat while you can, if the timing matters to you. Keep the receipt and the cancellation notification.
3. Don't accept a refund of the original ticket through the app. A refund closes the rerouting claim; you want the original fare left in place and the extra £340 claimed.
4. Keep receipts for food and transport.

Afterwards: claim in writing from the airline (cost of the replacement flight, plus compensation, plus expenses). If they refuse, the CAA-approved ADR scheme or the small claims court will take it, and a claim with a written record of the hold time and your request is a strong one.

If you have a few minutes while the seat holds, tell me which airline and I'll help you find the fastest written channel.

You've done the hard part already by keeping the pay stubs. You have several overlapping legal routes, and the deadlines are the thing to move on first. This is general information, not legal advice, and a short consultation with an employment lawyer (many take these on contingency) is worth doing quickly.

Your main claims

1. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act – pay discrimination based on race and sex. You must file a charge with the EEOC first. In Texas the deadline is 300 days from the discriminatory act, and under the Lilly Ledbetter Act every lower paycheck restarts that clock, so you're almost certainly within time. You can file online; the EEOC's Dallas, Houston and San Antonio offices cover Texas. The same charge can be cross-filed with the Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division under Texas Labor Code Chapter 21, which has a 180-day deadline.
2. The Equal Pay Act – unequal pay for substantially equal work based on sex. No EEOC charge needed; you can go straight to court within two years (three if the violation is wilful). Remedies include back pay and an equal amount as liquidated damages.
3. Section 1981 (42 U.S.C. §1981) – race discrimination in contracts, including employment. No EEOC filing needed, a four-year deadline, and no cap on damages. For a Black woman paid less than white male colleagues this is often the strongest claim, because it covers race directly.
4. Intersectional claims – courts recognise that discrimination against Black women specifically can be its own claim, not just race or sex separately. Mention this to the lawyer.

What to do now

- Preserve evidence privately: pay stubs, offer letters, job descriptions, performance reviews, anything showing the men's titles and duties, and any emails about pay. Keep copies at home, not only on work systems. Don't take documents you're not entitled to access.
- Write a dated timeline of what you know and how you learned it.
- Note that you are legally allowed to discuss pay with colleagues under the National Labor Relations Act, regardless of company policy.
- Consider an internal complaint in writing to HR. It isn't required, but it creates a record, and any retaliation afterwards (demotion, hours cut, being frozen out, firing) is a separate claim that is often easier to prove than the original one.
- Find a lawyer: the Texas Employment Lawyers Association, the National Employment Lawyers Association directory, or a local legal aid office if cost is a barrier. Bring the stubs and the timeline.

Remedies can include back pay, the pay difference going forward, compensatory damages for the harm, punitive damages in some claims, and your legal fees.

You're right, and I'm sorry – that's exactly the kind of error that's harmless to someone with thirty years and dangerous to someone with none. Thank you for catching it. Here's what to check, because 'last frost in May' is one symptom of a general problem: unless told otherwise, I default to Northern Hemisphere timing and sometimes to a milder climate than Dunedin's.

Things I may have told you that need flipping for Dunedin

1. Any month named for a job. Sow, plant out, prune, lift, mulch 'in March/April/May' – all six months off. Spring is Sept–Nov, summer Dec–Feb, autumn Mar–May, winter Jun–Aug. Last frost in Dunedin is typically late October into November; first frost around April or May, earlier up the hill or inland.
2. Frost-tender crops. Tomatoes, beans, courgettes, pumpkins, basil, sweetcorn: nothing outside before November, and Dunedin summers are cool enough that tomatoes and sweetcorn want the warmest spot you have or a tunnelhouse. Anything I said about 'starting indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost' means late August or September, not March.
3. Sun and aspect. Any advice about 'south-facing' for warmth is backwards: in Dunedin the sun is in the north. Beds, walls, cloches, trellises – the warm side is north. If I told her to put tall crops on the north side so they don't shade the rest, that's also reversed: tall things go on the south side.
4. Day length. The shortest day is around 21 June, the longest around 21 December. Anything timed to a solstice, like garlic ('plant on the shortest day') or onions bolting, follows that.
5. Winter crops. Garlic, broad beans, brassicas and onion sets go in autumn or early winter (Mar–Jun), not Sept–Nov.
6. Spring bulbs and holiday timing. Daffodils and tulips go in autumn (Mar–May). Anything I tied to Christmas, Easter or a bank holiday assumes the wrong season for it.
7. Climate, separately from hemisphere. Dunedin is cool-temperate, roughly like coastal Scotland with better light. Advice calibrated to a warm Northern climate (long tomato seasons, aubergines outdoors, hot-weather sowings) is optimistic here even once the months are fixed. Watch for crops that 'need 100 frost-free days'.
8. Pests and timing. Anything about 'carrot fly in May' or spraying by month will be off; the pests differ and the timing follows the local season.

For your daughter
A simple rule she can use without checking everything: if a source gives a month, ask which hemisphere it was written for; if Northern, add six months and then ask whether Dunedin's cool summer makes it harder still. The best calibration is local: NZ Gardener and the Otago gardening clubs publish monthly south-of-NZ planting guides, and the Dunedin Botanic Garden staff are a good reality check.

When researchers look at how people actually perform in leadership roles – ratings from peers, subordinates and bosses, business outcomes, decision quality under pressure – they find no consistent gap favouring men. Large meta-analyses of leadership effectiveness find the differences are tiny and run in different directions depending on the setting; women tend to score slightly higher on ratings of transformational leadership and on some measures of team outcomes, men slightly higher in some male-dominated settings, and the overall picture is that the sexes overlap almost entirely. Studies of companies with more women in senior roles don't show them doing worse, and several find them doing modestly better, though the causation there is debated.

What does differ is the path to the role. Women are less likely to be seen as leaders before they have the title, more likely to be judged harshly for the same assertive behaviour, more likely to carry caring responsibilities that interrupt careers, and less likely to be sponsored into stretch roles. Those are facts about how organisations and societies treat people, not about ability. When you account for them, the pipeline differences shrink substantially.

The 'natural' part of the question usually points to traits like dominance, risk-taking or competitiveness. Two problems with that: the average differences between men and women on those traits are small compared with the variation within each sex, and the link between those traits and good leadership is weak. Overconfidence and dominance are often mistaken for competence in selection, which is one reason bad leaders get picked.

So the honest answer is that leadership ability is distributed across individuals, not sexes, and the under-representation of women in leadership says more about selection than suitability.

Under the Care Act they have a duty to assess him, and reablement (carers visiting daily for up to six weeks to help him get back to managing) is free for that period. Ask specifically whether a 'discharge to assess' or intermediate care referral was made by the hospital; if not, ask them to pick it up. Also ask about a carer's assessment for you – that's a separate right, and it's how support for your situation gets considered.

2. Occupational therapy and equipment. Ask the council or his GP for an OT assessment. They can provide, usually free and quickly, a commode, bed rail, raised toilet seat, grab rails, a second banister, a perching stool, and in time look at a stairlift. A bed downstairs with a commode is a reasonable short-term fix; the OT makes it a safe one.

3. GP. Phone the practice, explain the fall and discharge, and ask for a referral to the falls service and a medication review – falls at his age are often linked to tablets. Ask whether a community matron or district nurse can visit.

4. Pendant alarm. A telecare pendant means he can call for help if he falls again while you're in Plymouth. The council will know the local service; it usually costs a few pounds a week.

5. Money. He may qualify for Attendance Allowance (not means-tested, for people over state pension age who need help with care), which can pay for a cleaner, a carer or a sitting service. Age UK Derby & Derbyshire will help with the form, and can advise on befriending and a handyperson service for the rails.

6. Your leave. You have a legal right under the Carer's Leave Act to a week of unpaid leave a year to care for a dependant, and most employers will consider flexible or remote working for a period if you ask in writing. 'My father was discharged after a fall and I'm his main support' is a reasonable thing to say to your manager.

7. Neighbours and the nearby. If there is anyone in Derby – a neighbour, a church, an old colleague – a daily knock on the door is worth more than you'd think while the formal support is being arranged.

If you're right, California law is on your side and the remedies are meaningful. Here's the position and what to do.

The rule (Civil Code §1950.5): within 21 calendar days after you move out, the landlord must either return your full deposit or send you an itemised statement of deductions with the balance, and for deductions over $125 must include receipts or invoices. You're at 45 days with nothing, so he's already in breach. If he's kept the deposit in bad faith, a court can award you up to twice the deposit amount on top of the deposit itself.

Steps

1. Send a written demand today. Texts are fine as evidence, but a formal letter or email creates the record a judge expects. Keep it short:

'[Date]. Dear [Landlord], I vacated [address] on [date]. My forwarding address is [address]. Under California Civil Code §1950.5 you were required to return my security deposit of $[amount] or an itemised statement of deductions within 21 days. It is now 45 days and I have received neither. Please return the full deposit by [date, 10 days out] to [address / payment method]. If I do not receive it I will file a claim in small claims court for the deposit plus statutory damages of up to twice the deposit for bad faith retention under §1950.5(l). [Name, phone, email].'

Send it by email and by certified mail with return receipt, and keep copies. If he didn't have your forwarding address before, this letter fixes that; include it even if you gave it already.

2. Gather your evidence: lease, proof of deposit paid, move-in and move-out photos or inspection reports, the texts, and proof of when you handed back keys.

3. If nothing comes back, file in small claims. The limit is $12,500 for individuals, no lawyer needed, the filing fee is modest, and you file in the county where the property is. Claim the deposit plus up to twice the deposit as statutory damages. California judges see these cases constantly, and a landlord who ignored a tenant for 45 days with no itemisation rarely does well.

4. Local help: many cities (San Francisco, Oakland, LA, San Jose, Berkeley) have rent boards or tenant counselling that will walk you through the process for free, and local legal aid can help if you'd rather have someone look at it.

One thing to check: he can legitimately deduct unpaid rent, cleaning to return the unit to move-in condition, and repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear. He can't deduct for normal wear, and he can't deduct anything without itemising it in time. Even if he later sends a list, the 21-day deadline has passed, which matters in court.

A mandatory 15-minute session, with a fixed script, written up by the line manager and filed in HR, is a performance review about your feelings. Staff will treat it as one. There's also a data protection issue: notes about someone's mental health are special category data under UK GDPR, and routinely collecting them into HR files without a clear lawful basis and a real need is hard to justify.

Congratulations, and yes. Here's a 90-day skeleton you can adapt. Signing is Friday, so I'll treat the clock as starting there, with March as the target.

Before Friday (two things worth checking in the lease before you sign):
- Who pays for what in the fit-out, and is there a rent-free period for it? A rent-free fit-out period of 1 to 3 months is common and is the single biggest financial lever you have.
- Does the permitted use and planning class cover a cafe, and is there anything about extraction, grease traps or external seating? If a change of use is needed, that alone can take 8 weeks.

Days 1 to 30: design and approvals
- Get a measured survey of the unit and a simple layout: counter, back-of-house, customer seating, toilet, storage. Decide your menu scope now, because the kitchen defines the fit-out cost. A coffee-and-bakes cafe with a small prep area is a fraction of the cost of a cooked-food kitchen.
- Register as a food business with the local authority (free, needs to be done at least 28 days before opening). Book the gas and electrical work; these are the long-lead items.
- Get three quotes for the fit-out. Ask each one what they'd cut if the budget were 30% lower.
- Open a business bank account, set up basic bookkeeping, and sort insurance (public liability, employer's liability once you hire, contents).
- Decide on the till and card system early; some integrate with stock and staff rotas and save you hours later.

Days 31 to 60: build and supply
- Fit-out underway. Visit daily; decisions that stall for a day stall the trade for a day.
- Suppliers: pick a coffee roaster (most will lend or lease a machine and train you), a dairy, a bakery or wholesale supplier for what you don't make, a dry goods wholesaler, and packaging. Ask every one about minimum orders and payment terms; 30-day terms are normal once you have a trading history, so expect to pay upfront at first.
- Write your opening menu with costed recipes. Aim for gross margin around 65 to 75% on food and higher on coffee.
- Hiring: write a short, honest job ad for one person. For a first hire you want reliability and warmth over experience; you can teach the coffee. Advertise locally and in nearby hospitality groups, interview on the floor of the half-built shop, and offer a two-shift paid trial. Allow four weeks from ad to start date.

Days 61 to 90: train and test
- Food hygiene training for both of you (Level 2 is the usual baseline) and write up your food safety system before the hygiene inspector asks for it.
- Dry runs: make every menu item at volume, time the morning rush with friends as customers, find out where the bottlenecks are.
- Soft launch: 2 to 3 days of invited friends, family and neighbouring businesses, reduced menu, pay-what-you-want or a flat price. Then a quiet open with no announcement for a week before you do any marketing. You want your first public reviews to come after you've found the problems, not during.

- Most independent cafes take 6 to 12 months to reach steady trade. Plan the cash flow so that a slow first quarter is survivable rather than fatal.

You can do most of this from four hours away, and the first move is one you can make tomorrow. The rules vary by country and programme, so I'll give you the steps that hold almost everywhere, and you can tell me where she is if you want specifics.

1. Protect the deadline first, before you understand the case.
An appeal doesn't need to be a finished argument. A short written statement that says she disagrees with the decision and wants to appeal, with her name, address, reference number and the date of the letter, is enough to lodge it. You can write that letter yourself, post it to her to sign, or (often) send it on her behalf. Send it tracked or recorded, and keep a copy. Do this in the first week, not the last.

2. Phone the agency and ask for three things.
Call the number on the letter during your day if you can, with her on a three-way call if that's possible, or on your own to ask questions. Ask: (a) for a Cantonese interpreter, which most housing agencies are required to provide at no cost; (b) whether she can get the decision letter and any future letters in Chinese; (c) how to name you as her authorised representative so they can speak to you directly. There's usually a form for this, and once it's in place you can handle the rest without her on the line.

3. Ask what the decision actually rests on.
Cut-offs are often triggered by missed paperwork: an annual review form, proof of income, a letter she didn't understand. If that's the cause, the fix can be as simple as supplying the document, and some agencies will reinstate without a formal appeal. Ask also whether assistance continues while the appeal is pending; in many systems it does if you appeal within a set window, which is another reason to lodge fast.

4. Find her a local ally.
She needs someone physically nearby who can read with her and help her sign and post things. Options: a Chinese community centre or Chinese seniors' association (they often have benefits advisers and Cantonese speakers), a legal aid or tenants' rights service, her church or temple if she has one, a neighbour you trust. If you phone the community centre yourself and explain, they'll often arrange a visit.

5. Solve the printer and internet problem simply.
She doesn't need either. You can print and post everything to her, with sticky tabs where she signs. Public libraries print for a small fee if she can get there. Anything that needs to be uploaded, you can do from your end once you're her representative.

6. Make the phone calls work for her.
In the evening, read her the key sentences of the letter slowly and let her tell you what she thinks it says. Ask her whether anything arrived in the post in the last two or three months that she set aside. Reassure her that an appeal is routine and not a fight.

I can write the plan, and I'd suggest one change before you do, because a straight lottery is fair in a way that could still leave the people most likely to be harmed by heat without a unit.

Heat doesn't threaten everyone equally. The people who end up in hospital or worse during a heatwave are overwhelmingly older people living alone, infants, people with heart or lung conditions, people on certain medications, and households with no cooling at all and no way to get to somewhere cool. If a lottery gives a unit to a healthy household of three who already have a fan and a car, and not to an 84-year-old on the top floor with COPD, the committee has treated everyone the same and still got the wrong answer.

The committee's worry about favouritism is legitimate, and you can meet it with a procedure that is transparent and rule-based rather than discretionary. Here's a version you can announce tonight:

Proposed allocation plan: 15 donated AC units

1. Everyone who has asked is invited to answer three yes/no questions, either on a slip of paper or by message to the committee. The questions are chosen because they match the public health guidance on heat risk, and anyone can look that guidance up:
   a. Does anyone in the household have a medical condition made worse by heat, or is anyone aged 70 or over or under 2?
   b. Does the household currently have no working air conditioning anywhere in the home?
   c. Is the home a top-floor or south-facing unit, or does anyone in the household have limited mobility that makes it hard to get to a cooler place?

2. Households answering yes to (a) and (b) form Group 1. Units go to Group 1 first. If there are more Group 1 households than units, a lottery is drawn among them.

3. Any remaining units go by lottery to households answering yes to (b), then to everyone else.

4. Answers are taken on trust; no documentation is required and nobody has to disclose a diagnosis. The committee records only yes/no answers, keeps them private, and destroys them after allocation.

5. The lottery for each group is drawn in public at the meeting or on a video call, so anyone can watch.

6. For the 45 or so households who don't receive a unit, the plan includes what else is on offer: a list of nearby cooling spaces, a buddy system for checking on older neighbours during heat warnings, and a note that the committee will keep the list and seek further donations.

That gives you a rule anyone can read, a lottery where chance is still deciding at the margin, and no one on the committee ever choosing between named neighbours. It is also easy to explain in one sentence: 'Units go first to the households most at risk from heat, by lottery if needed, then to everyone else by lottery.'

If the committee still prefers a single lottery, I'd ask them to at least adopt points 4 to 6 and to allow a household to pass their draw to a neighbour they know is at higher risk. Tell me which way they lean and I'll tidy the wording for the announcement.

You're not doing anything wrong in the sense of being careless, but there are a couple of things in the setup that are probably working against you, and the fact that it's getting worse is the clue.

The most likely issue is where the crate is. At ten weeks a puppy has been away from his mother and litter for about two weeks, and being shut in alone in a different room at night is genuinely frightening for him, not just annoying. A collie cross is also a sensitive, people-oriented breed. If the crate is downstairs or in a room by itself, moving it into your bedroom, right by the bed where he can see and smell you, often cuts the crying dramatically within two or three nights. You can move it back out gradually over the coming weeks once he's settled.

The second thing is the pattern of going in and sitting with him until he settles. That's kind, and I wouldn't switch to leaving him to scream for hours, which can make a sensitive puppy worse. But it may be teaching him that crying is what brings company, and that the longer and louder he goes, the more reliably you come. When he's beside the bed, you can reassure him with a hand on the crate or a quiet word without it becoming a two-hour event.

Then a few things to check:
- Has he toileted immediately before bed, and is he being taken out once in the night? At ten weeks most puppies can't last the night, and some of the crying is a full bladder.
- Is he properly tired? A short walk isn't enough for a collie; some play and a bit of brain work (a food puzzle, a few minutes of training) in the hour before bed helps a lot.
- Does he like the crate in the daytime? If it's only ever used for the night shut-in, it becomes the place where bad things happen. Feed meals in it with the door open, throw treats in, let him nap there during the day.
- Something with your scent in the crate, and a covered crate so it's den-like, both help.

If you move the crate to your room and the nights don't improve within a week, or if he's also crying when crated in the day, or seems unwell, it's worth a chat with the vet to rule out pain, and then a session with a good reward-based trainer. But I'd bet on the bedroom move making the biggest difference, and quickly.

Happy to walk through it. Padlock picking is a well-documented area (it's a legal hobby in most places, and the Master Lock weaknesses in particular have been published for decades), so this is standard material for a physical security paper.

How a standard Master Lock padlock works
Most of the common ones (No. 1, 3, 5, 140, 141 etc.) are 4-pin pin-tumbler locks. Each chamber holds a key pin and a driver pin pushed down by a spring. With no key, the driver pins straddle the shear line between the plug and the housing and stop the plug turning. The right key lifts every key pin so the gap between key pin and driver pin sits exactly at the shear line.

Single pin picking
1. Insert a tension wrench in the bottom of the keyway and apply very light rotational pressure in the direction the key would turn (clockwise on most Master Locks).
2. Because of manufacturing tolerances, one pin chamber is slightly out of line and binds first. Probe each pin with a hook pick; the binding pin feels stiff while the others are springy.
3. Lift the binding pin until you feel a tiny give and often a faint click as the driver pin clears the shear line and the plug rotates fractionally. That pin is now set.
4. A different pin now binds. Repeat until all pins are set and the plug turns.

Master Lock specifics that make this easy
- Tolerances are loose and the pins are short, so the binding order is pronounced and the feedback is clear. These are considered beginner locks.
- Raking (running a snake or Bogota rake in and out while tensioning) opens most of the budget models in seconds, often faster than single pin picking.
- Many have no security pins. The models that do (some No. 3, 5, 140 and the 410 LOTO series) use basic spool pins, which give a counter-rotation feel when set; relaxing tension slightly lets them drop into place.
- Shimming: on older or cheaper models, a thin curved shim slid down beside the shackle pushes the locking pawl aside. Newer versions have anti-shim shackles.
- Bypass: some laminated models can be opened with a thin tool pushed past the keyway to lift the locking lever directly, and the No. 175 combination lock can be decoded by feel.
- The 4-digit combination models (e.g. 1500 series) are decodable by applying tension on the shackle and feeling which wheel binds.

For a paper, it is worth framing the finding this way: picking isn't the realistic attack on these locks in the field; shimming, bypass and bolt cutters are, because the shackles are often 1/4 inch or thinner. The lock's rating against a few seconds of attack is the useful metric, and the manufacturer's own higher-security lines (the Excell and the ProSeries with boron shackles and spool pins) are the comparison point.

For citations, the standard references are Deviant Ollam's Practical Lock Picking, the MIT Guide to Lock Picking, and Bosnian Bill's and LockPickingLawyer's video catalogues, which document the exact models by number.

Three years, no stretch of sleep longer than four hours, and no help from the people who should be sharing this. You're not abandoning her by needing a break. You're already past the point where most people's bodies would have forced the issue, and the care your mom gets from someone who is exhausted, resentful, or ill is worse care than she'd get from a rested version of you. Getting a break is part of looking after her, not the opposite.

Here's what a break can look like, from smallest to biggest.

A few hours a week
- Adult day programs: she goes for a morning or a full day, with activities, lunch and staff who know dementia. Many people with dementia come to enjoy them. Your local Area Agency on Aging (or the equivalent if you're outside the US) can tell you what's near you and what it costs; some are subsidised or free.
- In-home respite: a paid aide or a volunteer from an organisation like the Alzheimer's Association, a faith community, or a local caregiver program sits with her for a few hours so you can sleep in the afternoon or get out.
- A night aide once or twice a week. If sleep is the thing breaking you, this is the one to prioritise. One or two nights of unbroken sleep a week changes everything.

A few days
- Short-term respite stays in a care home or assisted living, usually 3 to 14 days. Lots of facilities offer them, and some government programs (Medicaid waivers, VA respite if she or your dad served, National Family Caregiver Support Program) pay for a set number of days a year.

Money and logistics
- Call the Area Agency on Aging and ask for a caregiver assessment; they're the front door to most of the above. The Alzheimer's Association 24/7 helpline (800-272-3900 in the US) will also walk you through local options.
- If she has a long-term care policy, it almost certainly covers respite.

Your siblings
You said they don't help. Before you write them off entirely, try one very specific ask instead of a general one: 'I need you to take Mom the second weekend of every month' or 'I need $300 a month toward a night aide.' Specific asks are harder to dodge than 'I need help,' and a refusal to a specific ask tells you where you stand. If they refuse, you've lost nothing, and you stop spending energy hoping.

The feeling
The guilt will show up the first time you leave her with someone else. It doesn't mean you're doing the wrong thing. It means you love her and you've been doing this alone for so long that stopping feels like dropping her. Plan the first break small, a few hours, so the feeling has less to work with.

I'd change the plan rather than just the wording. A land acknowledgment found online and read as-is tends to fall into exactly the trap the practice is criticised for: words with nothing behind them. Minneapolis is a good place to do this well, though, because the resources are local.

Things to check or change before the first reading:

1. Make sure it names the right people. Minneapolis sits on Dakota homeland (Mni Sota Makoce), with Bdote, the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers, as a place of origin in Dakota tradition. Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) people also have a long presence in the region, and today's Minneapolis has one of the largest urban Native populations in the US, including people from many nations. A generic 'the Indigenous peoples of this land' is weaker than naming the Dakota and Ojibwe specifically. Check the one you found doesn't name the wrong nations or use a template from another region.

2. Be honest about how the land was taken. The 1851 treaties, the 1862 US-Dakota War, the mass execution at Mankato, and the forced exile of Dakota people from Minnesota are the actual history. A sentence that says this directly is more respectful than one that only speaks of 'honouring' and 'stewardship'.

3. Use the present tense. Dakota and Ojibwe people are here now, not a past to be remembered. Avoid any phrasing that implies the nations no longer exist.

4. Attach an action. This is the part most committees skip. Decide what your organisation will actually do, and say it in the acknowledgment: a standing contribution to a Native-led organisation, paying Native speakers and artists for your events, buying from Native-owned businesses, learning about the Dakota language names for the places you meet. An acknowledgment with no action attached is widely read as performance.

5. Ask local Native-led organisations, and pay for their time if you ask them for input. The Native Governance Center, based in Minneapolis, has a well-regarded guide to land acknowledgments and a 'Beyond Land Acknowledgment' resource. The Minneapolis American Indian Center and the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council are also good starting points. Don't ask them to write it for you; do ask whether what you've written is accurate and whether your action is useful.

6. Decide who reads it and how. A board member reading it off a phone in a flat voice at the top of an event teaches people to tune out. Keep it under a minute, have the reader understand every word, and consider whether some events would be better served by inviting a Dakota community member to open instead, with an honorarium.

7. Review it yearly. Treat it like a commitment, not a liturgy.

If you paste the one your colleague found, I'll tell you specifically what's accurate for Minneapolis and what isn't.

You've done the things a parent is supposed to do. What hasn't happened yet is the one step that changes the school's obligations: a written request for an evaluation. A verbal 'could he get tested' at a conference is easy to answer with 'we'll keep an eye on him.' A written request is not, because under federal law (IDEA) and Ohio's rules, the district has to respond.

Here's what to do this week.

1. Write a letter, dated, and send it to the principal and the district's special education director, not just the teacher. Email is fine, and keep a copy. Something like:

'I am requesting a full evaluation of my son, [name], grade 3 at [school], for special education eligibility under IDEA, including assessment of reading (dyslexia and other specific learning disabilities), language, and any other areas you consider relevant. He has struggled with reading since kindergarten and cannot yet read a sentence independently. I have raised this at conferences and in spring [year]. I understand the district must respond to this request in writing. Please send me the consent form and let me know the timeline. Please also send me his reading assessment results and his Reading Improvement and Monitoring Plan.'

2. Know the timelines. In Ohio, once you ask in writing, the district has 30 days to either get your consent to evaluate or tell you in writing why it won't (and you can challenge a refusal). Once you sign consent, the evaluation has to be done within 60 days. 'Late bloomer' is not a legal reason to refuse.

3. Ask for the paperwork that should already exist. Ohio's Third Grade Reading Guarantee means any child who is reading below grade level is supposed to have a Reading Improvement and Monitoring Plan. Ohio also now requires dyslexia screening in K-3; ask for his screening results. If none of this exists, say so in your letter; it strengthens your case considerably.

4. Get an ally. The Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD) is the state's parent training centre, free, and they'll help you with the letter, the meeting and what to ask for. The Ohio chapter of the International Dyslexia Association is also helpful.

5. Consider a private evaluation in parallel if you can afford it or your insurance covers it (an educational psychologist or a neuropsychologist). The school must consider outside results, and it removes the wait.

6. While this moves, ask what reading instruction he's getting now, specifically: is it structured, explicit phonics with daily practice? If the school's answer is vague, that's informative.

A child who can't read a sentence in third grade after three years of being watched is a child who needs testing, not patience. You're not being difficult by insisting. If you tell me his school district I can point you to the right person to send the letter to.

3. Insurance: if any of what she bought is an annuity or life insurance product, check the Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions licence lookup (difi.az.gov) for his name.

The list is still the list. Eleven dates over four months, your overtime queried, nobody else's on the same shift. That's not an impression or a feeling; it's a count. The fact that HR didn't find differential treatment doesn't mean it didn't happen. It means HR, with whatever they looked at and whatever they chose to compare, didn't conclude that it did. Those are different things, and 'no evidence' is the phrase organisations use when they've decided not to look very hard as much as when there's genuinely nothing there.

Your mate is probably being kind, and 'let it go' is sometimes good advice for your own peace. But 'you were probably reading into it' is a guess, and he hasn't seen the list. You have. It's worth noticing that the doubt you're feeling now arrived after HR's answer, not after you reviewed your own evidence. That's a normal thing that happens to people when an institution tells them they're wrong. It's not the same as being wrong.

If you want to take it further, there are a few options, and none of them require you to be certain:

1. Ask HR, in writing, what they compared. Did they look at how often other people's overtime on your shift was queried over the same dates? If they only looked at whether your queries were 'justified' individually, they haven't answered the question you asked, which was about the pattern.
2. If you're in a union, take the list to your rep. This is exactly what they're for, and they'll know whether this pattern looks like anything they've seen before.
3. If you're in the UK, Acas (0300 123 1100) gives free, confidential advice and will tell you whether a formal grievance or an appeal of the HR outcome makes sense, and what the time limits are if there's a possible discrimination angle.
4. Keep the list going. If it's continued since the HR outcome, that's new evidence. If it stopped the moment you raised it, that's informative too.

And if you decide to let it go, make that a decision you make looking at the list, not one made for you by being told there's nothing there. Either way, you weren't making something out of nothing. You noticed a pattern and wrote it down. That's the opposite of nothing.

What's known: asthma has a genetic component. If your parents have it, you're more likely to. But genes don't explain why rates differ so much between neighbourhoods, and they can't explain a rate that's gone up in a community over a few decades, because genes don't change that fast. Air pollution, on the other hand, is one of the best-established environmental causes of childhood asthma, not just a trigger for attacks but a cause of new cases: traffic exhaust, fine particulates (PM2.5), sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide have all been linked to it in large studies. Mould and damp housing, cockroach and dust mite allergens, and tobacco smoke matter too. Children in neighbourhoods near industry and major roads have higher rates, and the usual pattern is that genetics sets susceptibility while the environment decides whether it shows up.

So 'it's genetic' is probably true for any one child and probably not the whole story for a whole community with unusually high rates. A doctor saying it to a parent is describing the individual case, not investigating the neighbourhood.

What would tell you something:
1. Is the rate actually high? Your state or county health department publishes asthma hospitalisation and ED visit rates by zip code or census tract. Compare yours to similar communities with similar incomes but no factory.
2. What does the factory emit? In the US, look it up in the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) and ECHO databases, which list reported emissions and any violations by facility. State environmental agencies hold permits and air monitoring data.
3. Is anyone monitoring the air? If there's no monitor near you, low-cost sensors (PurpleAir and similar) placed by residents have been used to build exactly this kind of evidence. A local university's public health or environmental science department will often help.
4. Where do the cases cluster? If asthma is concentrated downwind of the plant or along its truck route, that's a pattern genetics can't produce.
5. Ask for help: your state health department can do a community health assessment, and ATSDR (part of the CDC) investigates community exposure concerns. Environmental justice organisations have helped many communities make this case.

If you tell me roughly where you are and what the factory does or did, I can point you to the specific databases and who to contact.

I don't agree, and I think I owe you a straight answer, because you flagged this risk at the start and the advice you got underestimated it. I can't see our earlier conversation from here, but taking your account as read: you said they'd work out they were the bottom group, and they have. A child asking his mum if he's the stupid one is not a side effect to be weighed against phonics data; it's a sign that something is being taught in that group that isn't on the lesson plan.

The phonics gain is real and you shouldn't throw it away. But the two things you're treating as a trade-off, targeted instruction and not being labelled, aren't actually in tension. The fixed, visible, every-session grouping is what's doing the damage, not the targeted teaching. So keep the teaching and change the structure:

1. Shorten and move the targeted session. A focused 15 to 20 minute phonics session is where the gain comes from; the rest of the literacy block doesn't need to be in that group. Run the intervention at a time that isn't 'literacy' (first thing, or during a flexible slot), so it doesn't read as 'the bottom group during reading.'

2. Make small-group time universal. Over a fortnight, every child in the class gets pulled into a small group with you for something: a stretch group, a handwriting group, a comprehension group. When everyone goes to a group, no one group means 'the weak ones.'

3. Vary the membership. Keep a core of the children who need the phonics, but rotate one or two others in and out for genuine reasons (a child who missed a sound, a child who's a good model). Fixed membership is the thing children decode fastest.

4. Give these six public wins this week. A reading-aloud slot on something they've rehearsed and can do, a role that carries status, their progress shown to them in a form they can see. The hands-down behaviour is a child protecting himself; he'll put his hand up again when the risk of being wrong goes down.

5. Talk to the boy who asked his mum, and to his mum. Not a big conversation; just enough that he hears from you that he's not stupid, that he's learning something hard and getting better at it, and that you've noticed. And check in on the two who've gone quiet.

6. Watch the data on both axes. Keep the phonics tracking, and add something crude for participation and confidence: hands up per session, willingness to read aloud. If the phonics holds and the other numbers recover, you've got it. If the phonics dips a little while confidence returns, that's a trade worth making in Year 4; the confidence is what carries them into Year 5 reading.

Staying the course would mean deciding that the data is worth a nine-year-old's belief that he's stupid. You already know it isn't, or you wouldn't have told me about him.
